name: Priya Alvarez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to AI firms, employers, unions, parties or government; we sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential. What does a normal shift involve?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I answer calls and chats when a gym membership was cancelled but the payment still went through. I have been at the contact centre for ten years, and I am steady on the usual billing cases, though the complex legal complaints go to a senior agent. I finished secondary school and earn the normal wage for this desk. I use approved AI search every day to find past messages, then check the live payment dates myself.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What about life after the shift?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I am 58 and live with my wife Selma, who works in a school kitchen. Our grown daughters have their own homes. We rent a flat and have five months of expenses saved. Several contact centres are within a reasonable journey. I would like to slow down eventually, but neither of us has worked out a wage replacement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau: Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the team that a short cancellation summary helps us find the date, but it cannot decide whether money left the customer’s account afterward. I check the payment line. A cancelled membership is not a refunded payment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect my work and Selma’s school-kitchen pay to hold. Five months saved covers a normal repair, so I would not change jobs over a small shortcut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I will keep taking cancellation calls and checking AI summaries against actual payments. In the first year I will replace the money we used from savings for the window repair by adding a little from each wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm. The window closes now, and the desk still needs somebody to look at the second debit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What did the assistant miss?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It found the cancellation request but not the charge posted the following Monday. I caught that when I opened the payment ledger.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you replace the window money?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Selma and I would transfer a fixed amount after each payday until the five-month cushion is whole again. We can wait on new curtains.

I would look for a **post-cancellation charge** before closing a case.
think: I expect both **household wages** to hold.
I know five months saved makes a **routine repair** manageable while both household wages still arrive.
do: Keep taking **cancellation calls** and check every AI summary against the actual payment date in the live ledger.
Restore **window-repair savings** from each wage before buying curtains.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption: Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say the company should count payments taken after an automatic cancellation, not only chats closed. A customer needs a person who can put the money back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could learn the new error screen quickly, but routine cancellation hours may shrink. Five months saved gives me a search window, not a reason to accept unpaid correction work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I will learn the new AI payment-audit screen by checking thirty closed cancellations during paid time. Two coworkers and I will take the wrong-charge count to our staff association and ask together for paid appeal hours. If my hours fall in the first year, I will apply for posted paid complaints roles nearby only when their full weekly wages and hours cover rent after travel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about a smaller week. Knowing the error count gives us a specific demand, not a promise of more shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you accept a role with a better title?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Selma and I would compare the journey and the full paid week first. A nicer title can still leave less after bus fare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would the staff association act?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We would sign one request for written appeal hours and a direct customer callback route. The three of us would not just show a chart and go home.

I would ask for **paid appeals** with coworkers.

I fear **routine hours** shrinking despite five months saved.

Ask through **staff association** for written paid appeal hours and callbacks.
Apply after cuts for **posted paid complaints** with rent-covering weekly wages and hours after travel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028: Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would warn that full thinking AI by 2028 could read the account and settle most cancellations without us. Hands-on robots around 2031 are later and do not protect a billing screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect our cancellation team could close, including my place. Five months saved matters, but Selma’s kitchen pay will not carry the rent indefinitely if I lose mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I will ask for written staffing dates and put a planned family trip on hold. If my calls end in the first year after 2028, I will check posted paid community-centre reception work and move only for weekly wages and hours covering rent after bus travel. I will also ask our staff association to press together for notice and paid redeployment terms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel alarmed by the possible whole-team loss. Savings are a bridge, not a replacement employer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Have you done reception work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I help at the community centre’s weekend reading group, but that is unpaid. I would ask what an actual paid reception shift involves before saying I can do it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you spend savings on a course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not on a course with no paid opening attached. If the centre needs a new booking system, I would learn it during paid work from someone there.

I would separate **2031 robots** from desk risk.

Five months saved cannot replace my **wage** indefinitely.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031: Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say five years lets us see which jobs actually pay before the calls change. General AI reaches cancellations in 2031 and hands-on robots follow around 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could learn the community desk while the centre still pays me, but visitors may use automated booking too. I would treat it as a paid bridge, not a safe forever job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I will keep my calls and ask the community centre for any posted paid reception rota. If it offers weekly wages covering rent after bus travel, I will learn its room-booking rules on a paid shift. In the first year after 2031 I will move only when the paid hours are real and Selma’s school-kitchen rota still works with our shared morning travel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious, but there is time to inspect a real workday. A room-booking screen is not a pay packet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you seek a certificate?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I need someone at the desk to show me the keys and booking book during paid hours. The posting, not a badge, would tell me there is work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask the association?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We would keep asking for written redeployment openings, not only training lists. Workers cannot pay rent with a list.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036: Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say a decade is time to keep earning and negotiate a real path for people whose calls shrink. General AI reaches billing in 2036, with hands-on robots around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 68 I may want to work fewer shifts, but Selma and I have not settled what replaces my wage. Five months saved is useful, not a retirement date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I will keep the cancellation calls and put a small share of each pay toward six months saved. Every year I will compare posted community and contact-centre roles by full weekly wages. If my calls fall in the first year after 2036, I will move only for paid work covering rent after travel, while Selma keeps her kitchen shifts if possible.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy about the far date, steady enough today to build the reserve. More time helps when the wages actually arrive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you leave before then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not on a guess. We have no confirmed income to replace both wages, and the rent comes every month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your daughters contribute?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They have families and bills of their own. We would enjoy their visits without treating their earnings as our plan.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most. The cancellation desk could close before a paid reception place appears. Written notice, paid redeployment terms and a posted job with enough weekly pay after travel would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who can reopen a charge after the assistant says the membership ended. A closed chat does not return a payment. Someone needs paid time and authority to put it right.

headlineQuote: A closed chat does not return a payment.
portrait: Priya is a **58-year-old experienced agent** with secondary schooling, average skill and typical pay.
She uses **AI daily** but checks live payments; her wife works in a school kitchen.
With **five months saved** and some nearby centres, she can inspect paid alternatives before moving.
She seeks **joint paid redeployment** and treats community volunteering as distinct from a posted wage.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could close her cancellation desk before paid reception work opens.
whatWouldHelp: **Written notice**, paid redeployment and a posted job with rent-covering weekly pay would help.
